question: In its communication entitled ‘Labour and skills shortages in the EU: an action Plan’ (COM(2024) 131 final) of 20 March 2024, the Commission states that the response to labour shortages must first be to mobilise the untapped potential of the EU labour force (increasing the activity rate, upskilling, improving working conditions and intra-EU mobility), but points out that attracting talent from third countries must also be part of the solution.

At the same time, the communication entitled ‘Demographic change in Europe: a toolbox for action’ (COM(2023) 577 final) of 11 October 2023 stresses that higher productivity, the digital transition and technological developments are key levers in addressing the ageing of the population and safeguarding European competitiveness. In view of the above: 1.

What quantitative assessments has the Commission carried out to determine the potential impact of robotisation, artificial intelligence and productivity gains on labour shortages compared with the impact of increased legal migration?

Does it intend to set European targets that prioritise automation, robotisation and greater use of artificial intelligence in sectors under pressure, before resorting to increased migration from third countries?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.11.2026)

The Commission acknowledges the need to address labour and skills gaps as part of wider efforts to boost Europe’s sustainable prosperity and competitiveness1. Recent evidence showcases labour shortages as a cause of weak productivity growth and a consequence of demographic change, and, in some sectors, poor working conditions, reflecting challenges to improve job quality and productivity in certain firms2.

Labour shortages can be addressed by untapping current potential and by integrating AI and robotics into core business processes. The Apply AI Strategy3 sets up concrete actions to support AI uptake and development including through AI-powered robotics. The Commission will further provide access to AI literacy trainings through the AI Skills Academy4.

The AI observatory will provide indicators to assess the impact of AI and monitor developments and trends. A digitally skilled workforce is a prerequisite for a responsible uptake of AI. The EU Digital Decade Policy Programme 20305, and the Union of Skills6 aim to strengthen skills and digital literacy. However, AI and untapping labour potential may not be enough to address these shortages.

Facilitating legal migration is crucial for boosting the EU's competitiveness. The Commission will support Member States and companies with measures for legal migration based on the skills needs of our economies7. To this end, the Regulation establishing an EU Talent Pool8 and the Talent Partnerships9 will facilitate legal migration for non-EU nationals.
